name: Amira Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at Mount Selwyn, the iron ore mine up on the plateau. My job is keeping the haul roads smooth, so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres, which cost more than my house. I start at six with a pre-start check, then I'm up and down the same eight kilometres of road all day, cutting the ruts, spreading the gravel, and the water cart comes behind me. It's satisfying when a road is perfect. The tiring part is the concentration, because a 200-tonne truck coming the other way doesn't brake for you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Viktor and I had a café on Market Street for fifteen years. When the mine had its big downturn a few years back, half the town stopped buying coffee and we went under. We still owe the bank for the coffee machine and the fit-out, so there's not much left over, maybe a couple of weeks of bills in savings. Viktor drives a delivery van now and I came here at fifty-four, which is three, nearly four years ago. I'm still not quick on the grader, but I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's good news for people like us, who don't need more surprises. I'd probably say at break that the computer people got excited over nothing. Online I mostly share recipes, so I'd leave it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I get time, which is what I need most. I'm not fast, but every month nothing changes is a month I get better and the café loan gets smaller. That's how I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep paying the loan, the way we planned. I'd ask my supervisor, Joe, to let me do the steeper ramps more often so I learn them. Maybe I'd start a little weekend catering again in a year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you might restart catering. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small things, birthday cakes, trays of pastries for funerals and christenings. I used the AI on my phone last month to work out how much to charge, and it was quite helpful, actually. Just enough to put a hundred a week aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job that would still worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The autonomous trucks, a bit. They've got some running on the west roads already. But they still need someone to keep the roads good for them, maybe even better, because a robot truck doesn't like a pothole. So in a way they need me more.

S0.say: She'd say a plateau is good news for people who don't need more surprises and that the computer people got excited over nothing.
S0.think: She thinks it gives her time, which she needs most: each month without change is a month she gets better and the café loan shrinks.
S0.do: Keeps working and paying off the café loan as planned. Asks to work the steeper ramps more to improve, and considers restarting weekend catering in about a year.
S0.quote: I'm not fast, but every month nothing changes is a month I get better and the café loan gets smaller.
S0.fieldNote: Amira measures time in loan payments and skill gains, so a plateau is simply more runway. She's a cautious occasional AI user who found it handy for pricing catering work. She even reasons that self-driving trucks might need good roads, and so need her more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be sensible, find out what the company plans and make a plan of our own. I'm not one for shouting. I'd say it at the crew meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think graders get automated not long after the trucks. Once you have robot trucks on the roads, a robot grader is the obvious next step. I spent fifteen years watching the coffee machine, now I'd spend my last working years watching my grader drive off without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask in the first month whether there'll be training for the automated graders and put my name down. I'd restart the catering right away instead of waiting, so we have a second income. And we'd try to pay off the café loan faster, even if it means no holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can manage it, but it's there every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for training. How do you feel about learning those systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not the first person to try things, but once I see others doing it, I'm alright. My niece showed me how to use the AI for the catering and I picked it up. If two or three of the others are doing the automation course and it's working, I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about Viktor in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Delivery vans, that's another job everyone says will go. If he lost his and I lost mine in the same few years, we'd be back where we were when the café closed. That's my real nightmare, both at once.

S1.say: She'd say people need to be sensible, find out the company's plans and make their own, raising it calmly at the crew meeting.
S1.think: She believes graders will be automated soon after the trucks, and imagines her grader driving off without her as the café machine did.
S1.do: Puts her name down for automated grader training in the first month, once she sees colleagues doing it. Restarts the catering business immediately and pays the café loan faster, skipping holidays.
S1.quote: I spent fifteen years watching the coffee machine, now I'd spend my last working years watching my grader drive off without me.
S1.fieldNote: Amira's worry has two parts, her job and Viktor's delivery van going at once, which echoes the café closure. Her 'once others have' attitude shows clearly: she'd train if colleagues were already doing it successfully. Her first move is a second income, not a protest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and companies have to work together on this, quickly, because it's too big for families alone. I'd say keep calm and help each other. I'm not someone who'd march, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I'd think we'd be in real trouble. Me at sixty, Viktor at sixty-two, both jobs gone, the bank loan still there. We survived the café closing by taking any job going. In this one there'd be no 'any job' left to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away: phones, the car insurance down to basic, no eating out. I'd push the catering as hard as I could, while people still want a human cake. And we'd ask the bank to freeze the loan and go to the council for any support, before we needed it, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'while people still want a human cake'. Do you think they would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For weddings and funerals, maybe. People want to know Auntie made it. It wouldn't be a living, but it might be the last thing a robot doesn't get. I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, is there anything you'd do in those two years that you wouldn't otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying extra on the loan and put it in savings instead, so we'd have cash in hand. If everything goes, cash is what you need. Then I'd talk to our son about whether we might have to move in with him, which nobody wants.

S2.say: She'd say government and companies must act together quickly because it's too big for families, urging people to stay calm and help each other; she'd sign petitions but not march.
S2.think: She thinks she and Viktor would be in real trouble, both jobs gone and the loan still owing, with no 'any job' left to take this time.
S2.do: Cuts spending immediately and pushes the catering hard. Asks the bank to freeze the loan, seeks council support early and switches extra loan payments into cash savings.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: We survived the café closing by taking any job going. In this one there'd be no 'any job' left to take.
S2.fieldNote: Amira's response is practical and early: freeze the loan, build cash, apply for help before the crisis. The line about 'no any job' captures how this differs from the café closure. She is unsure whether handmade food would survive, and says so honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, if people take it seriously from day one. I'd tell the younger women at work to get qualifications now. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me sixty-three. If I can clear the café loan in three years, I can face the robots with nothing owing, and that changes everything for me. I think it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: every spare cent onto the loan, catering at weekends to speed it up. I'd do the automated grader course once the first group comes back and says it's useful. And I'd start a little savings jar for after, maybe from year three when the loan's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, so it's bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years to clear the loan with catering at weekends sounds tight. What's the number?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We owe about eleven thousand. If I put two hundred a month extra from catering and we keep our normal payment, it's about three years. Viktor says I'm too optimistic, but I'm usually right about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years make you think about leaving the mine for something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because there's nothing else here. The mine is the town. I'd rather be the person who knows the new grader than start again at a supermarket that'll also have robots.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough time to plan if people take it seriously from day one, and encourage younger women at work to get qualifications now.
S3.think: She thinks clearing the café loan within three years would let her face automation with nothing owing, which would change everything.
S3.do: Puts every spare cent and about two hundred a month of catering money onto the loan for three years. Takes the automated grader course once the first group reports back, and starts saving after the loan is cleared.
S3.feel: Anxious but bearable, because there's a plan.
S3.quote: If I can clear the café loan in three years, I can face the robots with nothing owing, and that changes everything for me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years transforms Amira's outlook into a debt plan with real numbers, and she's confident she's right about money. She sees no alternatives in town and chooses to stay and learn rather than switch jobs. Her advice to younger women at work is one of the few times she speaks beyond her household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if we're sensible, and there's no need to panic. I'd tell my son to plan his career with it in mind. Not much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm sixty-eight. I'd be retired or close to it. Ten years means the robots arrive at my retirement party, not my job interview. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the loan, then save for retirement properly. I'd learn the new grader systems when the others do. And I'd keep the catering going so I have something to do and a bit of money once I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the young ones, but for me it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think about your pension much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than I'd like. It'll be the state pension and a small amount from the mine's scheme, since I came late. If the catering brings in a little and Viktor works a few more years, we'll be fine, not comfortable, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he should pick work where people want a person, nursing or teaching, or fixing the robots. He's an electrician, so maybe he's alright. I'd tell him to get every certificate he can while he's young.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are sensible and there's no need to panic, advising her son to plan his career around it.
S4.think: She thinks she'd be retired or close to it at sixty-eight, so AGI would arrive at her retirement party, not her job interview.
S4.do: Clears the café loan, then saves for retirement. Learns new grader systems alongside colleagues and keeps the catering going for money and something to do after she stops.
S4.feel: Manageable for herself, uneasy for young people.
S4.quote: Ten years means the robots arrive at my retirement party, not my job interview.
S4.fieldNote: A decade puts Amira's working life largely out of harm's way, and her vivid line about the retirement party shows the relief. Her pension will be thin because she started late, and she's honest that 'fine' is not comfortable. Her concern moves to her son, who she thinks may be safer as an electrician.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Viktor and I would lose both jobs while we still owe the bank. What would help is the government letting people over fifty-five freeze business debts if they lose their jobs to automation, and a bit of help to start something small, like my catering. Practical help, not speeches.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. When the mine had a bad year, my café died. If the mine goes, every café, every hairdresser, every school goes with it. People forget that.

headlineQuote: When the mine had a bad year, my café died. If the mine goes, every café, every hairdresser, every school goes with it.
portrait: Amira Ziegler is 58 and grades the haul roads at the Mount Selwyn iron ore mine, a job she took nearly four years ago after the café she ran with her partner Viktor failed in a mining downturn. They still owe the bank for the café, have about two weeks of savings, and Viktor now drives a delivery van. She is careful, practical and good with money, calm in a plateau and anxious in steady change, when her first step is to restart weekend catering. The two-year picture alarms her because both their jobs could go while the loan remains. With five or ten years she has a debt plan with real numbers and expects automation to arrive near her retirement.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Viktor could both lose their jobs while still owing the bank for the old café.
whatWouldHelp: Letting older workers who lose their jobs to automation freeze business debts, and help to start something small like her catering.
